scales.reach: How widely known the advice is (was 'commonality'). 1 rare, 5 universal. Low reach is not bad: niche advice that should be better known is the point of tracking it.
scales.ease: How easy it is to do (was 'practicality' / 'ease of implementation'). 1 impractical, 5 effortless.
scales.impact: How big the effect is thought to be. 1 minimal, 5 game-changer.
scales.novelty: How surprising it is. 1 obvious, 5 feels like a secret.
scales.evidenceSupport: How well research supports it (the wiki's 'scientific red flags', flipped). 1 red flag, 5 strongly supported.

taggingTaxonomy.title: Sleep Advice Coding Ideas (Advice Tagging Taxonomy v1.2)

mechanism.label: How it is said to work

body-clock.label: Body clock timing
body-clock.definition: Sets or shifts the circadian clock: light at the right time, regular times, gradual shifts, melatonin timing.

light-at-night.label: Light at night
light-at-night.definition: Less light in the evening or at night, said to keep melatonin up and the brain less alert.

sleep-pressure.label: Sleep pressure
sleep-pressure.definition: Builds or protects the drive to sleep that grows the longer you are awake (naps, time in bed, activity).

body-temperature.label: Body temperature
body-temperature.definition: Helps the core body temperature drop that comes with sleep (cool room, warm bath then cooling, warm feet).

arousal.label: Calming body and mind
arousal.definition: Lowers mental, emotional or physical arousal: stress, racing thoughts, exciting content, hard exercise.

learned-association.label: Learned cues
learned-association.definition: Trains the brain to link bed and bedtime routines with sleep, not with lying awake.

substances.label: Substances
substances.definition: Caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, supplements, herbal products, medicines.

digestion-and-fluids.label: Food, drink and digestion
digestion-and-fluids.definition: Meal timing and size, reflux, night-time bathroom trips.

sleep-environment.label: Bedroom environment
sleep-environment.definition: Noise, comfort, tidiness, scent: the room itself.

breathing-and-airway.label: Breathing and airway
breathing-and-airway.definition: Keeping the airway open at night; snoring and sleep apnea.

time-displacement.label: Time taken from sleep
time-displacement.definition: An activity that pushes bedtime later or eats into sleep time (e.g. screens, per Bauducco et al. 2024).

monitoring-and-care.label: Tracking and getting care
monitoring-and-care.definition: Noticing patterns or problems and getting them checked: sleep diaries, medicine reviews, testing for apnea.

items.sourceWording: Maintain a consistent sleep schedule
items.plain: Go to bed and get up at about the same times every day.

paragraph.text: Set a regular bedtime and wake-up time, even on weekends. Use alarms or bedtime reminders to help stay consistent, and get morning sunlight to reinforce your body’s natural clock.

evidence.summary: Numerous peer-reviewed studies confirm that a regular sleep schedule strengthens the body’s circadian rhythm, leading to improved sleep quality and overall health.[11] Disrupting sleep patterns can cause circadian misalignment, increasing the risk of metabolic disorders, cardiovascular disease, and cognitive decline. Health organizations like the CDC and NIH strongly recommend maintaining a consistent sleep-wake cycle.

evidence.summary:
Sudden shifts in sleep and wake times disrupt the body’s circadian rhythm, leading to negative effects on cognitive function, metabolism, and overall health. Research indicates that irregular sleep patterns can cause circadian misalignment, increasing the risk of obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and mood disorders[97]. The body's internal clock relies on consistent light exposure and melatonin secretion to regulate sleep-wake cycles, and erratic sleep schedules interfere with these natural processes, resulting in poor sleep quality, daytime fatigue, and impaired focus[11].

Health organizations, including the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the National Sleep Foundation, emphasize the importance of maintaining a stable sleep schedule [6],[98]. Keeping a consistent sleep-wake cycle supports brain function, hormone regulation, and physical performance while reducing the risks associated with chronic sleep deprivation and metabolic dysfunction.

paragraph.text: Set your thermostat between 60–67°F (15–19°C) for optimal sleep. If you don’t have air conditioning, use a fan, breathable bedding, and light pajamas to stay cool.

evidence.summary: Studies indicate that maintaining an optimal sleep temperature, typically between 60–67°F (16–19°C), can enhance sleep quality by supporting the body's natural thermoregulation process[45][46]. As bedtime approaches, the body's core temperature naturally drops, signaling that it's time to sleep. A cooler room helps facilitate this process, making it easier to fall asleep and stay asleep. Conversely, a room that is too warm can cause discomfort, increased wakefulness, and disruptions in deep sleep stages, leading to a less restorative sleep experience.

paragraph.text: If blackout curtains are too expensive or impractical, try an eye mask to block out light.

evidence.summary:
Light exposure plays a crucial role in regulating the body’s circadian rhythm, which controls sleep-wake cycles. Studies show that even small amounts of artificial light at night can disrupt melatonin production, leading to difficulty falling asleep, frequent awakenings, and reduced sleep quality. Exposure to streetlights, car headlights, or electronic devices can suppress melatonin levels, making it harder to maintain deep, restorative sleep.

Blackout curtains are designed to block external light sources, creating a dark sleep environment that supports melatonin release and helps regulate circadian rhythms. Research has linked sleeping in a dark environment to improved sleep efficiency, increased REM sleep, and better overall health. Disrupted sleep due to light exposure has been associated with an increased risk of obesity, metabolic disorders, and mood disturbances. Health organizations like the National Sleep Foundation recommend reducing nighttime light exposure to enhance sleep quality and long-term well-being.

paragraph.text: If a new mattress isn’t an option, try a mattress topper for added comfort or a pillow suited to your sleep position (firm for side sleepers, softer for back sleepers).

evidence.summary:
A good mattress and pillow are essential for maintaining proper spinal alignment, reducing pressure points, and promoting deep, uninterrupted sleep. Research shows that an uncomfortable or unsupportive sleep surface can contribute to musculoskeletal pain, frequent awakenings, and reduced sleep quality. Poor sleep due to an inadequate mattress has been linked to an increased risk of chronic pain, stress, and even cardiovascular issues.

Mattresses and pillows play a crucial role in regulating body temperature and pressure distribution during sleep. Memory foam, latex, and hybrid mattresses are known to provide better weight distribution, reducing tossing and turning throughout the night. Similarly, the right pillow supports the head and neck, preventing stiffness and discomfort that could disrupt sleep. Studies suggest that sleep surfaces tailored to an individual’s needs can improve sleep efficiency, decrease sleep disturbances, and enhance overall restfulness.

items.plain: If noise wakes you, try a fan or white noise to cover it.

paragraph.text: If a machine is not available, alternatives like a fan, air purifier, or low-volume static from a radio can provide a similar effect.

evidence.summary:
White noise machines can improve sleep quality by masking disruptive sounds and creating a consistent auditory environment. Research shows that unpredictable noises, such as traffic, barking dogs, or household activity, can cause frequent awakenings and fragmented sleep. White noise works by producing a steady sound that reduces the contrast between background noises, making sudden disturbances less likely to wake you.

Studies have demonstrated that white noise can shorten the time it takes to fall asleep, increase sleep efficiency, and enhance overall sleep satisfaction. In hospital settings, where noise pollution is a common issue, white noise has been shown to help patients sleep more soundly despite surrounding disturbances. Additionally, consistent sound exposure during sleep can improve slow-wave sleep, which is crucial for memory consolidation, immune function, and overall well-being.

A structured bedtime routine helps signal to the body that it’s time to wind down, making it easier to fall asleep and stay asleep. Activities such as reading, taking a warm bath, or practicing deep breathing stimulate the parasympathetic nervous system, which counteracts stress and promotes relaxation. evidence.summary:
Breathing through the nose rather than the mouth during sleep is essential for optimal oxygen exchange, sleep quality, and overall health. Nasal breathing helps filter, warm, and humidify the air, reducing the risk of airway irritation and promoting efficient oxygen absorption. In contrast, chronic mouth breathing has been linked to lower oxygen saturation, increased snoring, disrupted sleep cycles, and even sleep apnea.

Research indicates that mouth breathing can contribute to dry mouth, increased risk of cavities, throat irritation, and a higher likelihood of waking up throughout the night. Additionally, nasal breathing supports the production of nitric oxide, a molecule that enhances oxygen delivery to cells, reduces inflammation, and improves cardiovascular function— all of which contribute to better sleep and overall well-being.

evidence.summary:
- #### Truth: While alcohol may induce drowsiness and help you fall asleep faster, it negatively impacts the quality of your rest[77][78].

Alcohol disrupts the normal sleep cycle by reducing REM (rapid eye movement) sleep, which is essential for cognitive function, memory consolidation, and emotional regulation. As the body metabolizes alcohol, sleep becomes more fragmented, leading to frequent awakenings throughout the night. This results in grogginess, reduced alertness, and impaired performance the next day, despite feeling initially sleepy after drinking.

Additionally, alcohol can contribute to sleep disorders such as insomnia and sleep apnea[79][80]. It relaxes the muscles in the throat, increasing the likelihood of airway obstruction, which can lead to snoring or more severe breathing interruptions. Over time, relying on alcohol as a sleep aid can lead to dependency, further worsening sleep problems[78][81]. Instead of using alcohol to wind down, healthier alternatives such as reading, meditation, or maintaining a consistent bedtime routine can promote better sleep quality without negative side effects.

evidence.summary:
- #### Truth: Sleeping in on weekends may provide temporary relief from sleep deprivation, but it does not fully restore the negative effects of lost sleep[82][83].

Chronic sleep debt affects cognitive function, mood, metabolism, and overall health, and trying to compensate with extra sleep on weekends can create an irregular sleep pattern. This inconsistency can disrupt the body's circadian rhythm, making it harder to fall asleep and wake up at regular times during the week. Studies show that even after catching up on sleep, individuals may still experience impaired alertness, reduced reaction time, and difficulty concentrating.

Moreover, relying on weekend sleep-ins can contribute to a cycle of poor sleep habits. Late wake-up times on weekends often lead to staying up later at night, making it even harder to return to an early bedtime when the workweek begins[84]. This phenomenon, sometimes referred to as "social jet lag," can have long-term consequences on health, including an increased risk of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. Instead of trying to make up for lost sleep on weekends, maintaining a consistent sleep schedule—going to bed and waking up at the same time every day—is a more effective strategy for overall sleep health.

items.plain: Regular exercise helps sleep, but hard workouts right before bed can keep you up.

paragraph.text: Regular exercise is well known for promoting better sleep by reducing stress, improving mood, and regulating the body's circadian rhythm[17]. However, engaging in intense workouts too close to bedtime can have the opposite effect.

evidence.summary:
- #### Truth: Regular exercise is well known for promoting better sleep by reducing stress, improving mood, and regulating the body's circadian rhythm[17]. However, engaging in intense workouts too close to bedtime can have the opposite effect.

High-intensity exercise raises heart rate, core body temperature, and adrenaline levels, which can make it harder to relax and fall asleep[85]. The body's natural cooling process, which signals the brain that it's time to rest, can be delayed when exercise is performed late at night, leading to difficulties in sleep onset and reduced sleep quality.

To maximize the sleep benefits of exercise, it is best to finish vigorous workouts at least three hours before bedtime[86][87]. This allows the body enough time to cool down and shift into a more relaxed state conducive to sleep. Lighter forms of physical activity, such as yoga or stretching, can be beneficial before bed, as they promote relaxation without overstimulating the nervous system. Establishing a consistent exercise routine earlier in the day can enhance overall sleep quality and ensure a smoother transition into restful sleep at night.

paragraph.text: Many people believe that watching TV before bed helps them unwind and fall asleep, but it can actually do more harm than good[88].

evidence.summary:
- #### Truth: Many people believe that watching TV before bed helps them unwind and fall asleep, but it can actually do more harm than good[88].

The blue light emitted by screens interferes with the body’s natural production of melatonin, the hormone responsible for regulating sleep. When melatonin levels are suppressed, it becomes harder to feel sleepy, leading to delayed sleep onset and reduced sleep quality[18][19]. Even if someone manages to fall asleep with the TV on, the stimulating content—whether it’s an engaging show, fast-paced action, or loud sounds—can keep the brain active, making sleep more fragmented and less restorative.

A better alternative is to establish a relaxing, screen-free bedtime routine. Engaging in activities such as reading a book, practicing mindfulness, or listening to calming music can help signal the body that it's time to rest[76]. Dimming the lights and reducing exposure to screens at least an hour before bed allows melatonin levels to rise naturally, leading to easier sleep initiation and deeper, more restorative rest. Creating a consistent nighttime routine without screen distractions can improve overall sleep quality and help maintain a healthy sleep-wake cycle.

items.sourceWording: Myth: Snoring is harmless.
items.plain: Loud, frequent snoring can be a sign of sleep apnea and is worth checking.

paragraph.text: Occasional snoring is common and may result from factors like nasal congestion, sleep position, or fatigue[89][90]. However, frequent and loud snoring can be a warning sign of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), a serious sleep disorder in which breathing repeatedly stops and starts during sleep[91].

evidence.summary:
OSA occurs when the muscles in the throat relax excessively, causing a temporary blockage of the airway. These pauses in breathing can lead to sudden drops in oxygen levels, triggering the brain to wake the person momentarily—often without them realizing it. This repeated disruption prevents deep, restorative sleep, leading to daytime fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and increased irritability.

Left untreated, sleep apnea can have significant long-term health consequences. The repeated oxygen deprivation and sleep fragmentation put extra strain on the cardiovascular system, increasing the risk of high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes[92][93]. Additionally, untreated sleep apnea has been linked to weight gain, weakened immune function, and a higher likelihood of accidents due to excessive daytime sleepiness[94]. If snoring is loud, persistent, or accompanied by gasping, choking, or pauses in breathing, it is essential to seek medical evaluation. Lifestyle changes, such as maintaining a healthy weight, adjusting sleep position, or using a CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) machine, can help manage sleep apnea and improve overall health.[95][96]
